common_name: White Gold Bleeding Heart (Chartreuse-Gold Foliage, White Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring while soil is cool; in zone 9 plant September-February for establishment before summer heat arrives and the plant goes dormant.

directions: White Gold arose as a spontaneous seedling selection (PP27638) combining the bright chartreuse-gold spring foliage of 'Gold Heart' with pure white, pendant, heart-shaped flowers in April-May. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, since the golden leaves scorch in direct sun. Like other bleeding hearts it goes summer-dormant once heat arrives, so interplant with ferns or hostas to fill the gap.
sources: Pleasant Run Nursery — Plant Variety Database
U.S. Patent and Trademark Office — Plant Patent Records

common_name: Ruby Gold Bleeding Heart (Gold Foliage, True Red Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, humus-rich soil; in zone 9 plant in fall through winter so roots establish before the brief spring bloom and display before summer dormancy.

directions: A Terra Nova Nurseries introduction pairing the golden foliage of 'Gold Heart' with true red flowers held on reddish stems, giving a bushier, more vigorous plant with a longer bloom season than the species. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, as gold foliage scorches in strong sun. Flowers attract hummingbirds; the plant dies back after flowering and returns the following spring.

common_name: Adrian Bloom Western Bleeding Heart (Compact Crimson-Rose Selection)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this compact selection resents summer heat and drought.

directions: A compact Pacific bleeding heart selection, named for the Blooms of Bressingham plantsman, growing just 10-12 inches tall with deeply cut, grayish-green ferny foliage and nodding, rich crimson-rose flowers in spring. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade, where its small stature suits the front of a woodland border or shaded rock garden. Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation — Native Plant Database

common_name: Pearl Drops Western Bleeding Heart (Pale Pink-White Fernleaf Selection)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in shade; foliage scorches and the plant goes dormant early if the site dries out.

directions: A soft-colored Pacific bleeding heart selection bearing pale pink, nearly white, heart-shaped flowers over finely dissected, blue-green fernlike foliage from mid- to late spring. Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the gentle coloring pairs well with hostas, ferns, and other pastel woodland companions. Spreads gradually by shallow rhizomes to form a loose colony over time.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Dicentra

common_name: Snowflakes Fringed Bleeding Heart (White-Flowered Reblooming Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat in zone 9.

directions: A white-flowered selection of the native fringed bleeding heart, carrying clean white, dangling, heart-shaped blossoms above finely cut, blue-green ferny foliage from mid-spring and intermittently into summer wherever soil moisture is maintained. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade alongside ferns and hostas. Unlike the common Asian bleeding heart, it does not go fully summer-dormant and self-sows modestly to form a naturalized patch.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Dicentra
American Horticultural Society — Perennial Plant Guide
